**Lesson 99: In Brief**

This first lesson is in the form of an introduction. It is followed by the narratives (qisas) and, at the end, by conclusions and commentary. In this introductory part, all the foundational matters of the Islamic worldview and its basic truths are stated: worship and obedience belong to Allah alone, the One without partner, and religion belongs to Allah alone. It is necessary to believe that one day we shall all stand before Allah for reward, punishment, and accountability, and that this reckoning will be based on the good and bad deeds performed in this world, because this world is the abode of trial.

In this introduction, the knowledge of Allah and His attributes is presented from the angle of how powerfully His Being and attributes operate in this universe. This lesson also informs the believers about the reality of the Divine Being and His sovereignty, about human worship and obedience to Him, and about the demands of that relationship. The demand of human servitude is that just as a person is a servant of Allah in this world, so too will he be His servant in the Hereafter.

This introduction also discusses the establishment of prophethood and the reality of the Messenger. The Messenger is addressed and consoled: the opposition of the deniers to your call, their challenges, and their baseless hostility are nothing unusual. As we have said, in the entire history of da'wah (the call to Islam), Makkah was the most difficult period for the Prophet (ﷺ), and the polytheists did not accept the Qur'an as the Word of Allah. In response, the polytheists were told that if they do not accept this Qur'an as the Word of Allah, then let them produce ten surahs like it, as they claimed they could. In this way the Messenger (ﷺ) was consoled that they could never produce speech like this Qur'an. Thus this challenge was also a source of reassurance for those who had already believed.

Along with this consolation, the deniers of the truth are given a clear warning: the punishment they are asking to be hastened is very painful and awaits them. Their condition is such that when even a minor hardship comes upon them in this world, they cannot bear it, although compared to the punishment of the Hereafter, every worldly hardship is trivial.

This warning is also presented in the form of a scene from the Day of Resurrection. In this scene it is shown that the polytheists, the deniers, their associates, and their intercessors will be unable in any way to save them from the punishment on the Day of Judgment, while the believers will be in Gardens, and blessings and honors will be their portion. This scene, in the distinctive manner of the Qur'an, is extremely vivid and visual, and it appears to be moving before the eyes. The Qur'an says:

﴿The likeness of the two parties is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in likeness? Will you not then take heed?﴾ (11:24)

**Explanation of Verses 1–24**

**Explanation of Verses 1–4**

In these verses the following truths are stated, which are the fundamental truths of the religion of Islam:

- The proof of revelation and prophethood.
- The affirmation that worship belongs to Allah alone.
- Those who follow this revelation and guidance will have reward in this world and the Hereafter, on the condition that they adopt this guidance as a system of life.
- Those who deny it will deserve punishment. Whether one is obedient or a denier, one must stand before Allah one day.
- The power and dominion of Allah are unlimited; He has power over everything.

*Alif-Lam-Ra*: this is the subject, and its predicate is the whole sentence that follows: ﴿A Book whose verses are made firm, then made detailed, from One who is All-Wise and All-Aware﴾. The meaning is that this Book is composed of the same letters that are within people's reach, and those who deny it are challenged: if they are told to produce a book like it from these same letters, they are unable to do so.

﴿A Book whose verses are made firm, then made detailed, from One who is All-Wise and All-Aware﴾. Its verses are firm, meaning they have a strong structure and profound meaning. Every letter and every command is purposeful; every concept and every guidance is intended and meaningful. Each of its indications points to a target, and these verses are highly harmonious and interconnected; the outlook and vision of all its verses is one. Then, its verses are detailed, divided according to subject and purpose, arranged in categories, and each verse is placed in its appropriate position.

The question arises: who arranged these verses in such a firm composition and such eloquent meaning? Let it be remembered that Allah, glorified is He, did this Himself; the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had no role in the composition and organization of these verses. It is from ﴿One who is All-Wise and All-Aware﴾. This Book describes Allah's commands and also provides their necessary details. It was revealed by Allah in exactly the form that is before us today, and no alteration or change has occurred in it at any point.

And what fundamental doctrine is presented in these verses? The foundation of its teachings is this statement: ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾. That is, the system of life should be Allah's, worship should be to Allah, and obedience and sovereignty should be Allah's, exclusively and solely.

﴿Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good news﴾. This is the concept of prophethood, and the great purpose of prophethood is to give the good news of Allah's rewards and to warn against an evil end.

﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾. That is, abandon polytheism, disbelief, and disobedience, return to Allah, and accept Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and the Islamic system of life.

﴿He will give you good provision for an appointed term, and will give every person of merit his merit﴾. This is the reward for those who repent and seek forgiveness.

﴿But if you turn away, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great Day﴾. This is a warning for those who turn away from the call.

﴿To Allah is your return﴾. This expresses the belief that all will ultimately be presented before Allah.

﴿And He is Able over all things﴾. This mentions Allah's absolute power, and that He is capable of doing everything.

These are the aims of the Book of Allah, and its verses point to them. These are the fundamental beliefs and concepts upon which the edifice of the Islamic system of life has been raised.

Every person should keep well in mind that no religion or system can be established on this earth, and no civilization or culture can succeed in the world, unless it answers these fundamental questions. Every philosophy and system of thought in the world must necessarily answer these questions.

The belief that in the world all forms of worship belong to Allah alone closes all the paths on which a human being goes astray, falls into confusion, and becomes entangled in ideological and intellectual aberration. Humanity can be freed from baseless fancies, superstition, false ideologies, and the worship and slavery of false gods only if it is made a slave of Allah alone. In the world we have designated certain persons and things which we regard as intermediaries between Allah and the servant, and these persons spiritually lead people astray. There are certain people and institutions which we have accepted as rulers and supreme authorities, and these people run the worldly lives of human beings according to their own wishes. They take for themselves the most exclusive attributes of Allah, namely sovereignty and the authority of supreme power. In this way they make people slaves of those false and fabricated gods, which is manifest polytheism (shirk jali).

Unless the belief in Tawhid is established and refined in this broad sense in the world, no collective, political, economic, moral, national, or international system can be established in which a person may be freed from becoming a tool of the desires, rationalizations, and personal aims of other human beings.

Apart from establishing the belief in Tawhid, a human being cannot attain the freedom and dignity that Allah has designated for him, nor can he be freed from the humiliation, fear, and restlessness that always beset him. The belief in Tawhid can be completely established only when Allah is acknowledged in these meanings: as Lord (Rabb), as the One worthy of worship (Ma'bud), as the Creative Ruler and Governor (takwini hakim wa mudabbir), and as the Legislative Ruler and Lawgiver (tashri'i hakim wa qanun-saz), and when the human being is completely excluded from this domain of authority, so that he has no role or influence in these matters.

In the entire history of humanity, the conflict between Islam and jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance and rejection of guidance), and the historic struggle between the truth (haqq) and the taghut (every power that transgresses against Allah's sovereignty), has not been over whether Allah is the God and Lord of this universe, and that it is He alone who manages it through His cosmic laws. Rather, this battle and this dispute were over the question: who is the Lord of mankind? Whose system and law shall be enforced upon people? And whom should people obey, and whose commands, especially political commands, should they accept?

The taghut powers of this world usurped this right of Allah and continued to enforce their own laws and decrees in people's lives, thus removing people from the sovereignty of Allah and bringing them into the domain of their own sovereignty. The objective of all the prophets, all the messages, and all the Islamic movements has always been this: to remove people from the domain of authority usurped by these taghut powers and bring them into the government of Allah, the kingship of Allah, and the sovereignty of Allah.

Allah is the King, free from need of all the worlds. The disobedience and rebellion of people cannot diminish His dominion even by a hair's weight, and even if all creation were to unite in His worship and accept His rule, His kingdom could not increase by a hair's weight. But when people accept the sovereignty of anyone or anything other than Allah, they themselves become humiliated, wretched, and enslaved. And if they accept the political and ideological sovereignty of Allah alone, this itself becomes a source of honor and dignity for them. They attain freedom in place of slavery and exaltation in place of lowliness, and no human being remains a slave of another human being or of a non-human. Since Allah wishes to see His servants honored, dignified, and exalted, He sent the messengers so that they might grant them this honor and dignity, and free them from the slavery of their fellow servants. In short, if there is any good in the Islamic worldview and the Islamic system, it is for human beings themselves; Allah is self-sufficient and free from need of all the worlds.

The level of dignity that Allah wishes to see in human life, and the height to which He wishes to raise it, cannot be reached until all people resolve to throw off from their necks the yoke of slavery to other than Allah, because the chain of slavery to other than Allah is a source of humiliation for a human being, whatever form it may take.

Religion will be purely for Allah only when people acknowledge Allah alone as Lord. And the meaning of Allah's lordship (rububiyyah) is that people adopt Allah's system, Allah's constitution, and Allah's laws and decrees. This is the truth that has been defined at the very beginning of this surah: ﴿A Book whose verses are made firm, then made detailed, from One who is All-Wise and All-Aware. That you worship none but Allah﴾.

This is the meaning of worship (ibadah) as the Arabs, in whose language the Qur'an was revealed, understood it well. Now the second important question arises: how is this sovereignty of Allah to be established? Its only way is for people to affirm prophethood (risalah), because this doctrine and system of divine sovereignty has been presented by Allah alone, and to accept prophethood means that whatever the Messenger brings, he brings from Allah. If the teachings of a messenger are not accepted as coming from Allah, then the sanctity and reverence that those teachings hold in the human conscience is lost. For if these teachings are regarded as coming from a messenger, then however much one may respect the messenger, that value of the teachings does not find a place in the human heart and mind, and a person does not respect those teachings in matters great or small. When the awareness that these teachings are from Allah settles in a person's heart and sight, then this awareness follows him at every moment, and he turns to Allah. It is this awareness that keeps the God-fearing and the obedient from straying from the straight path.

Moreover, through the affirmation of prophethood alone is determined the source and the standard from which a person can derive all those guidances that relate to the Islamic system and religion. This is the only path through which the taghut powers can be eliminated. Their method of operation is to fabricate on their own some law, standard, or doctrine, and then claim that it is from Allah, although they themselves have composed all of it.

The history of every jahiliyyah is this: some people arose, made their own law and standards, invented customs and traditions for the people, and then said that these were from Allah. This confusion can be ended in the name of Allah only if one believes in a messenger and accepts his words as coming from Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 11, verses 1–4 (part 2 of 2):

Here seeking forgiveness and repentance from shirk has been mentioned because seeking forgiveness is evidence that there is feeling within the heart. It is active against evil, it is conscious of sin, and it is inclined towards returning and turning back. However, along with feeling and consciousness, true repentance is that a person also practically abandons this sin and actually engages in good deeds in place of evil ones. Without giving up sins and doing righteous action, there is no concept of repentance. There are two practical signs of repentance. These two conditions are the interpreters of repentance, and the practical existence of repentance is realised only in these two forms, and only after such repentance can hope for forgiveness be entertained. If someone supposes that he has repented from shirk and has entered Islam, but after that he does not practically obey Allah, does not accept the Islamic system, and does not take the values and priorities of life from Islam, then this kind of assumption and supposition has no reality, and his practice denies his declaration, because in practice he accepts the systems of the tyrant (taghuti) powers.

The fundamental means of prophethood consists of two things. Giving good news (bashharah) and warning (nadhārah), showing good reward for the righteous and a bad end for the wicked, is the basic task of prophethood. Allah has created man and Allah is well aware of human psychology, so frightening people with a bad end and giving the good news of a good end leaves deep effects on man and creates in him the impulse to act.

The belief in accountability in the Hereafter is also necessary and true, and as a result there arises the awareness regarding this life that it is a purposeful and wise life, and that the goodness towards which all the messengers have been calling is the real aim and purpose of life. Therefore, a person will certainly receive the reward for accepting the call of the messengers, both in this world and in the Hereafter. And if he receives no recompense in this world, he will certainly receive it in the Hereafter, where this life will be completed. Those people who adopt crookedness towards the Islamic system and adopt deviation in their lives make themselves deserving of punishment. With this concept, sound nature (fitrah salimah) walks on the straight path and does not adopt deviation. And if it ever walks on the path of deviation, the door of repentance is open, so that it does not happen that it drowns in disobedience. Through attention and turning towards Allah, the life of a person is set right, and the direction of life can be turned towards goodness and virtue. The belief in the Hereafter, by itself, is not the cause of the reward of the Hereafter, as some people think; rather this belief moves a person to act in this world and establishes him on a life of righteousness and purity. And in this way a person attains the life that is desired by Allah. This manner of life befits man, and through it man can be distinguished from other animals. The concept that Islam has given of man is that Allah has created him in a special way. Then He has breathed into him His special spirit and has given him preference over all His creation. And in this way He has raised him above the station of animality, so that the aims of his life may be higher than those of animals, and his inclinations and purposes may be slightly superior to mere animal inclinations and purposes.

This is the purpose and objective because of which, in this Book of firm verses, after the doctrine of Tawhid, the establishment and obedience of the Islamic system, the belief in prophethood and following the Messenger, the call has been given: O people, repent from shirk and return to Allah. This is the path to establishing righteous action and a pure life. The meaning of righteous action is not that a person does some good deed and that is all; rather its purpose is that within the person there should be effort in accordance with every meaning of reform on this earth, effort should be made for the cultivation and construction of this earth, and its produce should be increased, both in this world and in the Hereafter. And when a nation attains this station of reform, then this reward is given to it.

"Yumatti'kum matā'an ḥasanan ilā ajalin musamman wa yu'ti kulla dhī faḍlin faḍlah" — "He will provide you with a good provision for a specified term, and will give to every person of merit his merit." In this world, the good provision (matā' ḥasan) is sometimes in terms of its kind and sometimes in terms of its quantity. And in the Hereafter it will be in terms of both kind and quantity, and it will be of such a degree that no one can even imagine it. However, we wish to say something about the good provision of this world.

In this world we see that many pious, righteous and repentant people, with great hardship and bitterness, keep body and soul together in this worldly life, although these verses contain a clear promise from Allah of good provision. We hear this question from countless people.

To understand the meaning contained in this verse, it is necessary that we try to understand life in its broader sense, seeking to understand it beyond its apparent circumstances and according to a wider and deeper meaning.

The reality is that in any society in which a righteous system is implemented, which is founded upon belief in Allah, in which obedience and submission are to Allah alone, in which Allah alone is recognised as the Lawgiver and Legislator, and in which people possess good deeds and character, then inevitably that society becomes developed, its facilities of life become abundant, and that society generally presents a model of a pure and clean life. In such a society every individual receives wages according to his effort. The members of that society are content, and prosperity is attained by them. And on the contrary, when we see that in some society the righteous and pure-natured people are passing their time with great difficulty, and they are counted among those deprived of goods and sources of sustenance, then the inevitable situation will be that the edifice of that society is not built upon belief in Allah, its system is not just, and in that entire society no person receives compensation according to his effort.

But it is also a reality that if righteous and virtuous people are living a narrow and bitter life in terms of wealth and sustenance, and oppression is being inflicted upon them by the society in which they exist, and they are being pursued from every side, as the polytheists of Makkah were inflicting oppression upon a small community of Muslims at the time of the revelation of this surah, and as every jahiliyyah always treats the bearers of the call of Islam in this same way, then we can say that these people are living a good life. This is not merely an idea or a claim, because connection with Allah, tranquillity of heart, peace from the Hereafter, and hope in the grace and mercy of Allah are in reality better provision. And for those people whose gaze rises a little above sensory and material life, this spiritual wealth is a greater good provision.

We do not say this because those people who do not receive, justly and equitably, their wages and good provision in accordance with their labour should abandon the struggle for good provision. For Islam never accepts oppression. And seeing such circumstances, a believer can never remain silent; Islam demands of a believing individual and a believing community that they continue the effort and struggle to change such conditions, so that righteous and virtuous workers may obtain good provision in accordance with their labour. Rather, we say that a righteous individual should be conscious of his rights, and should not accept the situation in which he continues to act and to labour but is not given its recompense and wage. It is their duty to create conditions in which pious and God-fearing people receive their full rights.

"Wa yu'ti kulla dhī faḍlin faḍlah" (and to every person of merit, his merit be given). Some exegetes have restricted this to the merit of the Hereafter. I consider that it relates to both this world and the Hereafter, just as we have explained "al-matā' al-ḥasan." Every person of excellence receives a reward as soon as he manifests his excellence. He attains psychological and conscious happiness. Whether this merit is practical or financial, if it is for the sake of Allah, then the reward is received at that time. The reward that will be given by Allah for it will be merit upon merit and will be the best of recompense.

"Wa in tawallaw fa innī akhāfu 'alaykum 'adhāba yawmin kabīr" (and if you turn away, then I fear for you the punishment of a great and terrible day). This is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. Some exegetes have said that it refers to the punishment of the Day of Badr. But this view is not correct, because the phrase "yawm kabīr," if used without qualification, means the Day of Resurrection, and the following sentence strengthens this view.

"Ilā Allāhi marji'ukum" (to Allah is your return). Although the return is to Allah both in this world and the Hereafter, and every moment and every instant a person returns to Allah, yet according to Quranic expressions the intended meaning is the state after the life of this world.

"Wa huwa 'alā kulli shay'in qadīr" (and He has power over all things). This clause also indicates that the great day mentioned refers to the Day of Resurrection, because on it people will be raised again, which the polytheists of Arabia considered far-fetched, and therefore it was said that Allah has power over all things.

**Lesson 99: In Brief**

This first lesson is in the form of an introduction. It is followed by the narratives (qisas) and, at the end, by conclusions and commentary. In this introductory part, all the foundational matters of the Islamic worldview and its basic truths are stated: worship and obedience belong to Allah alone, the One without partner, and religion belongs to Allah alone. It is necessary to believe that one day we shall all stand before Allah for reward, punishment, and accountability, and that this reckoning will be based on the good and bad deeds performed in this world, because this world is the abode of trial.

In this introduction, the knowledge of Allah and His attributes is presented from the angle of how powerfully His Being and attributes operate in this universe. This lesson also informs the believers about the reality of the Divine Being and His sovereignty, about human worship and obedience to Him, and about the demands of that relationship. The demand of human servitude is that just as a person is a servant of Allah in this world, so too will he be His servant in the Hereafter.

This introduction also discusses the establishment of prophethood and the reality of the Messenger. The Messenger is addressed and consoled: the opposition of the deniers to your call, their challenges, and their baseless hostility are nothing unusual. As we have said, in the entire history of da'wah (the call to Islam), Makkah was the most difficult period for the Prophet (ﷺ), and the polytheists did not accept the Qur'an as the Word of Allah. In response, the polytheists were told that if they do not accept this Qur'an as the Word of Allah, then let them produce ten surahs like it, as they claimed they could. In this way the Messenger (ﷺ) was consoled that they could never produce speech like this Qur'an. Thus this challenge was also a source of reassurance for those who had already believed.

Along with this consolation, the deniers of the truth are given a clear warning: the punishment they are asking to be hastened is very painful and awaits them. Their condition is such that when even a minor hardship comes upon them in this world, they cannot bear it, although compared to the punishment of the Hereafter, every worldly hardship is trivial.

This warning is also presented in the form of a scene from the Day of Resurrection. In this scene it is shown that the polytheists, the deniers, their associates, and their intercessors will be unable in any way to save them from the punishment on the Day of Judgment, while the believers will be in Gardens, and blessings and honors will be their portion. This scene, in the distinctive manner of the Qur'an, is extremely vivid and visual, and it appears to be moving before the eyes. The Qur'an says:

﴿The likeness of the two parties is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in likeness? Will you not then take heed?﴾ (11:24)

**Explanation of Verses 1–24**

**Explanation of Verses 1–4**

In these verses the following truths are stated, which are the fundamental truths of the religion of Islam:

- The proof of revelation and prophethood.
- The affirmation that worship belongs to Allah alone.
- Those who follow this revelation and guidance will have reward in this world and the Hereafter, on the condition that they adopt this guidance as a system of life.
- Those who deny it will deserve punishment. Whether one is obedient or a denier, one must stand before Allah one day.
- The power and dominion of Allah are unlimited; He has power over everything.

*Alif-Lam-Ra*: this is the subject, and its predicate is the whole sentence that follows: ﴿A Book whose verses are made firm, then made detailed, from One who is All-Wise and All-Aware﴾. The meaning is that this Book is composed of the same letters that are within people's reach, and those who deny it are challenged: if they are told to produce a book like it from these same letters, they are unable to do so.

﴿A Book whose verses are made firm, then made detailed, from One who is All-Wise and All-Aware﴾. Its verses are firm, meaning they have a strong structure and profound meaning. Every letter and every command is purposeful; every concept and every guidance is intended and meaningful. Each of its indications points to a target, and these verses are highly harmonious and interconnected; the outlook and vision of all its verses is one. Then, its verses are detailed, divided according to subject and purpose, arranged in categories, and each verse is placed in its appropriate position.

The question arises: who arranged these verses in such a firm composition and such eloquent meaning? Let it be remembered that Allah, glorified is He, did this Himself; the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had no role in the composition and organization of these verses. It is from ﴿One who is All-Wise and All-Aware﴾. This Book describes Allah's commands and also provides their necessary details. It was revealed by Allah in exactly the form that is before us today, and no alteration or change has occurred in it at any point.

And what fundamental doctrine is presented in these verses? The foundation of its teachings is this statement: ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾. That is, the system of life should be Allah's, worship should be to Allah, and obedience and sovereignty should be Allah's, exclusively and solely.

﴿Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good news﴾. This is the concept of prophethood, and the great purpose of prophethood is to give the good news of Allah's rewards and to warn against an evil end.

﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾. That is, abandon polytheism, disbelief, and disobedience, return to Allah, and accept Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and the Islamic system of life.

﴿He will give you good provision for an appointed term, and will give every person of merit his merit﴾. This is the reward for those who repent and seek forgiveness.

﴿But if you turn away, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great Day﴾. This is a warning for those who turn away from the call.

﴿To Allah is your return﴾. This expresses the belief that all will ultimately be presented before Allah.

﴿And He is Able over all things﴾. This mentions Allah's absolute power, and that He is capable of doing everything.

These are the aims of the Book of Allah, and its verses point to them. These are the fundamental beliefs and concepts upon which the edifice of the Islamic system of life has been raised.

Every person should keep well in mind that no religion or system can be established on this earth, and no civilization or culture can succeed in the world, unless it answers these fundamental questions. Every philosophy and system of thought in the world must necessarily answer these questions.

The belief that in the world all forms of worship belong to Allah alone closes all the paths on which a human being goes astray, falls into confusion, and becomes entangled in ideological and intellectual aberration. Humanity can be freed from baseless fancies, superstition, false ideologies, and the worship and slavery of false gods only if it is made a slave of Allah alone. In the world we have designated certain persons and things which we regard as intermediaries between Allah and the servant, and these persons spiritually lead people astray. There are certain people and institutions which we have accepted as rulers and supreme authorities, and these people run the worldly lives of human beings according to their own wishes. They take for themselves the most exclusive attributes of Allah, namely sovereignty and the authority of supreme power. In this way they make people slaves of those false and fabricated gods, which is manifest polytheism (shirk jali).

Unless the belief in Tawhid is established and refined in this broad sense in the world, no collective, political, economic, moral, national, or international system can be established in which a person may be freed from becoming a tool of the desires, rationalizations, and personal aims of other human beings.

Apart from establishing the belief in Tawhid, a human being cannot attain the freedom and dignity that Allah has designated for him, nor can he be freed from the humiliation, fear, and restlessness that always beset him. The belief in Tawhid can be completely established only when Allah is acknowledged in these meanings: as Lord (Rabb), as the One worthy of worship (Ma'bud), as the Creative Ruler and Governor (takwini hakim wa mudabbir), and as the Legislative Ruler and Lawgiver (tashri'i hakim wa qanun-saz), and when the human being is completely excluded from this domain of authority, so that he has no role or influence in these matters.

In the entire history of humanity, the conflict between Islam and jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance and rejection of guidance), and the historic struggle between the truth (haqq) and the taghut (every power that transgresses against Allah's sovereignty), has not been over whether Allah is the God and Lord of this universe, and that it is He alone who manages it through His cosmic laws. Rather, this battle and this dispute were over the question: who is the Lord of mankind? Whose system and law shall be enforced upon people? The disobedience and rebellion of people cannot diminish His dominion even by a hair's weight, and even if all creation were to unite in His worship and accept His rule, His kingdom could not increase by a hair's weight. But when people accept the sovereignty of anyone or anything other than Allah, they themselves become humiliated, wretched, and enslaved. The level of dignity that Allah wishes to see in human life, and the height to which He wishes to raise it, cannot be reached until all people resolve to throw off from their necks the yoke of slavery to other than Allah, because the chain of slavery to other than Allah is a source of humiliation for a human being, whatever form it may take.

Religion will be purely for Allah only when people acknowledge Allah alone as Lord. In this introductory part, all the foundational matters of the Islamic worldview and its basic truths are stated: worship and obedience belong to Allah alone, the One without partner, and religion belongs to Allah alone. It is necessary to believe that one day we shall all stand before Allah for reward, punishment, and accountability, and that this reckoning will be based on the good and bad deeds performed in this world, because this world is the abode of trial.

In this introduction, the knowledge of Allah and His attributes is presented from the angle of how powerfully His Being and attributes operate in this universe. This lesson also informs the believers about the reality of the Divine Being and His sovereignty, about human worship and obedience to Him, and about the demands of that relationship. The demand of human servitude is that just as a person is a servant of Allah in this world, so too will he be His servant in the Hereafter.

This introduction also discusses the establishment of prophethood and the reality of the Messenger. The Messenger is addressed and consoled: the opposition of the deniers to your call, their challenges, and their baseless hostility are nothing unusual. As we have said, in the entire history of da'wah (the call to Islam), Makkah was the most difficult period for the Prophet (ﷺ), and the polytheists did not accept the Qur'an as the Word of Allah. In response, the polytheists were told that if they do not accept this Qur'an as the Word of Allah, then let them produce ten surahs like it, as they claimed they could. In this way the Messenger (ﷺ) was consoled that they could never produce speech like this Qur'an. Thus this challenge was also a source of reassurance for those who had already believed.

Along with this consolation, the deniers of the truth are given a clear warning: the punishment they are asking to be hastened is very painful and awaits them. Their condition is such that when even a minor hardship comes upon them in this world, they cannot bear it, although compared to the punishment of the Hereafter, every worldly hardship is trivial.

This warning is also presented in the form of a scene from the Day of Resurrection. In this scene it is shown that the polytheists, the deniers, their associates, and their intercessors will be unable in any way to save them from the punishment on the Day of Judgment, while the believers will be in Gardens, and blessings and honors will be their portion. This scene, in the distinctive manner of the Qur'an, is extremely vivid and visual, and it appears to be moving before the eyes. The Qur'an says:

﴿The likeness of the two parties is like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in likeness? Will you not then take heed?﴾ (11:24)

**Explanation of Verses 1–24**

**Explanation of Verses 1–4**

In these verses the following truths are stated, which are the fundamental truths of the religion of Islam:

- The proof of revelation and prophethood.
- The affirmation that worship belongs to Allah alone.
- Those who follow this revelation and guidance will have reward in this world and the Hereafter, on the condition that they adopt this guidance as a system of life.
- Those who deny it will deserve punishment. Whether one is obedient or a denier, one must stand before Allah one day.
- The power and dominion of Allah are unlimited; He has power over everything.

*Alif-Lam-Ra*: this is the subject, and its predicate is the whole sentence that follows: ﴿A Book whose verses are made firm, then made detailed, from One who is All-Wise and All-Aware﴾. The meaning is that this Book is composed of the same letters that are within people's reach, and those who deny it are challenged: if they are told to produce a book like it from these same letters, they are unable to do so.

﴿A Book whose verses are made firm, then made detailed, from One who is All-Wise and All-Aware﴾. Its verses are firm, meaning they have a strong structure and profound meaning. Every letter and every command is purposeful; every concept and every guidance is intended and meaningful. Each of its indications points to a target, and these verses are highly harmonious and interconnected; the outlook and vision of all its verses is one. Then, its verses are detailed, divided according to subject and purpose, arranged in categories, and each verse is placed in its appropriate position.

The question arises: who arranged these verses in such a firm composition and such eloquent meaning? Let it be remembered that Allah, glorified is He, did this Himself; the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had no role in the composition and organization of these verses. It is from ﴿One who is All-Wise and All-Aware﴾. This Book describes Allah's commands and also provides their necessary details. It was revealed by Allah in exactly the form that is before us today, and no alteration or change has occurred in it at any point.

And what fundamental doctrine is presented in these verses? The foundation of its teachings is this statement: ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾. That is, the system of life should be Allah's, worship should be to Allah, and obedience and sovereignty should be Allah's, exclusively and solely.

﴿Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good news﴾. This is the concept of prophethood, and the great purpose of prophethood is to give the good news of Allah's rewards and to warn against an evil end.

﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾. That is, abandon polytheism, disbelief, and disobedience, return to Allah, and accept Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and the Islamic system of life.

﴿He will give you good provision for an appointed term, and will give every person of merit his merit﴾. This is the reward for those who repent and seek forgiveness.

﴿But if you turn away, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great Day﴾. This is a warning for those who turn away from the call.

﴿To Allah is your return﴾. This expresses the belief that all will ultimately be presented before Allah.

﴿And He is Able over all things﴾. This mentions Allah's absolute power, and that He is capable of doing everything.

These are the aims of the Book of Allah, and its verses point to them. These are the fundamental beliefs and concepts upon which the edifice of the Islamic system of life has been raised.

Every person should keep well in mind that no religion or system can be established on this earth, and no civilization or culture can succeed in the world, unless it answers these fundamental questions. Every philosophy and system of thought in the world must necessarily answer these questions.

The belief that in the world all forms of worship belong to Allah alone closes all the paths on which a human being goes astray, falls into confusion, and becomes entangled in ideological and intellectual aberration. Humanity can be freed from baseless fancies, superstition, false ideologies, and the worship and slavery of false gods only if it is made a slave of Allah alone. In the world we have designated certain persons and things which we regard as intermediaries between Allah and the servant, and these persons spiritually lead people astray. There are certain people and institutions which we have accepted as rulers and supreme authorities, and these people run the worldly lives of human beings according to their own wishes. They take for themselves the most exclusive attributes of Allah, namely sovereignty and the authority of supreme power. In this way they make people slaves of those false and fabricated gods, which is manifest polytheism (shirk jali).

Unless the belief in Tawhid is established and refined in this broad sense in the world, no collective, political, economic, moral, national, or international system can be established in which a person may be freed from becoming a tool of the desires, rationalizations, and personal aims of other human beings.

Apart from establishing the belief in Tawhid, a human being cannot attain the freedom and dignity that Allah has designated for him, nor can he be freed from the humiliation, fear, and restlessness that always beset him. The belief in Tawhid can be completely established only when Allah is acknowledged in these meanings: as Lord (Rabb), as the One worthy of worship (Ma'bud), as the Creative Ruler and Governor (takwini hakim wa mudabbir), and as the Legislative Ruler and Lawgiver (tashri'i hakim wa qanun-saz), and when the human being is completely excluded from this domain of authority, so that he has no role or influence in these matters.

In the entire history of humanity, the conflict between Islam and jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance and rejection of guidance), and the historic struggle between the truth (haqq) and the taghut (every power that transgresses against Allah's sovereignty), has not been over whether Allah is the God and Lord of this universe, and that it is He alone who manages it through His cosmic laws. Rather, this battle and this dispute were over the question: who is the Lord of mankind? Whose system and law shall be enforced upon people? And whom should people obey, and whose commands, especially political commands, should they accept?

The taghut powers of this world usurped this right of Allah and continued to enforce their own laws and decrees in people's lives, thus removing people from the sovereignty of Allah and bringing them into the domain of their own sovereignty. The objective of all the prophets, all the messages, and all the Islamic movements has always been this: to remove people from the domain of authority usurped by these taghut powers and bring them into the government of Allah, the kingship of Allah, and the sovereignty of Allah.

Allah is the King, free from need of all the worlds. The disobedience and rebellion of people cannot diminish His dominion even by a hair's weight, and even if all creation were to unite in His worship and accept His rule, His kingdom could not increase by a hair's weight. But when people accept the sovereignty of anyone or anything other than Allah, they themselves become humiliated, wretched, and enslaved. And if they accept the political and ideological sovereignty of Allah alone, this itself becomes a source of honor and dignity for them. They attain freedom in place of slavery and exaltation in place of lowliness, and no human being remains a slave of another human being or of a non-human. Since Allah wishes to see His servants honored, dignified, and exalted, He sent the messengers so that they might grant them this honor and dignity, and free them from the slavery of their fellow servants. In short, if there is any good in the Islamic worldview and the Islamic system, it is for human beings themselves; Allah is self-sufficient and free from need of all the worlds.

The level of dignity that Allah wishes to see in human life, and the height to which He wishes to raise it, cannot be reached until all people resolve to throw off from their necks the yoke of slavery to other than Allah, because the chain of slavery to other than Allah is a source of humiliation for a human being, whatever form it may take.

Religion will be purely for Allah only when people acknowledge Allah alone as Lord. And the meaning of Allah's lordship (rububiyyah) is that people adopt Allah's system, Allah's constitution, and Allah's laws and decrees. This is the truth that has been defined at the very beginning of this surah: ﴿A Book whose verses are made firm, then made detailed, from One who is All-Wise and All-Aware. That you worship none but Allah﴾.

This is the meaning of worship (ibadah) as the Arabs, in whose language the Qur'an was revealed, understood it well. Now the second important question arises: how is this sovereignty of Allah to be established? Its only way is for people to affirm prophethood (risalah), because this doctrine and system of divine sovereignty has been presented by Allah alone, and to accept prophethood means that whatever the Messenger brings, he brings from Allah. If the teachings of a messenger are not accepted as coming from Allah, then the sanctity and reverence that those teachings hold in the human conscience is lost. For if these teachings are regarded as coming from a messenger, then however much one may respect the messenger, that value of the teachings does not find a place in the human heart and mind, and a person does not respect those teachings in matters great or small. When the awareness that these teachings are from Allah settles in a person's heart and sight, then this awareness follows him at every moment, and he turns to Allah. It is this awareness that keeps the God-fearing and the obedient from straying from the straight path.

Moreover, through the affirmation of prophethood alone is determined the source and the standard from which a person can derive all those guidances that relate to the Islamic system and religion. This is the only path through which the taghut powers can be eliminated. Their method of operation is to fabricate on their own some law, standard, or doctrine, and then claim that it is from Allah, although they themselves have composed all of it.

The history of every jahiliyyah is this: some people arose, made their own law and standards, invented customs and traditions for the people, and then said that these were from Allah. This confusion can be ended in the name of Allah only if one believes in a messenger and accepts his words as coming from Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 11, verses 1–4 (part 2 of 2):

Here seeking forgiveness and repentance from shirk has been mentioned because seeking forgiveness is evidence that there is feeling within the heart. It is active against evil, it is conscious of sin, and it is inclined towards returning and turning back. However, along with feeling and consciousness, true repentance is that a person also practically abandons this sin and actually engages in good deeds in place of evil ones. Without giving up sins and doing righteous action, there is no concept of repentance. There are two practical signs of repentance. These two conditions are the interpreters of repentance, and the practical existence of repentance is realised only in these two forms, and only after such repentance can hope for forgiveness be entertained. If someone supposes that he has repented from shirk and has entered Islam, but after that he does not practically obey Allah, does not accept the Islamic system, and does not take the values and priorities of life from Islam, then this kind of assumption and supposition has no reality, and his practice denies his declaration, because in practice he accepts the systems of the tyrant (taghuti) powers.

The fundamental means of prophethood consists of two things. Giving good news (bashharah) and warning (nadhārah), showing good reward for the righteous and a bad end for the wicked, is the basic task of prophethood. Allah has created man and Allah is well aware of human psychology, so frightening people with a bad end and giving the good news of a good end leaves deep effects on man and creates in him the impulse to act.

The belief in accountability in the Hereafter is also necessary and true, and as a result there arises the awareness regarding this life that it is a purposeful and wise life, and that the goodness towards which all the messengers have been calling is the real aim and purpose of life. Therefore, a person will certainly receive the reward for accepting the call of the messengers, both in this world and in the Hereafter. And if he receives no recompense in this world, he will certainly receive it in the Hereafter, where this life will be completed. Those people who adopt crookedness towards the Islamic system and adopt deviation in their lives make themselves deserving of punishment. With this concept, sound nature (fitrah salimah) walks on the straight path and does not adopt deviation. And if it ever walks on the path of deviation, the door of repentance is open, so that it does not happen that it drowns in disobedience. Through attention and turning towards Allah, the life of a person is set right, and the direction of life can be turned towards goodness and virtue. The belief in the Hereafter, by itself, is not the cause of the reward of the Hereafter, as some people think; rather this belief moves a person to act in this world and establishes him on a life of righteousness and purity. And in this way a person attains the life that is desired by Allah. This manner of life befits man, and through it man can be distinguished from other animals. The concept that Islam has given of man is that Allah has created him in a special way. Then He has breathed into him His special spirit and has given him preference over all His creation. And in this way He has raised him above the station of animality, so that the aims of his life may be higher than those of animals, and his inclinations and purposes may be slightly superior to mere animal inclinations and purposes.

This is the purpose and objective because of which, in this Book of firm verses, after the doctrine of Tawhid, the establishment and obedience of the Islamic system, the belief in prophethood and following the Messenger, the call has been given: O people, repent from shirk and return to Allah. This is the path to establishing righteous action and a pure life. The meaning of righteous action is not that a person does some good deed and that is all; rather its purpose is that within the person there should be effort in accordance with every meaning of reform on this earth, effort should be made for the cultivation and construction of this earth, and its produce should be increased, both in this world and in the Hereafter. And when a nation attains this station of reform, then this reward is given to it.

"Yumatti'kum matā'an ḥasanan ilā ajalin musamman wa yu'ti kulla dhī faḍlin faḍlah" — "He will provide you with a good provision for a specified term, and will give to every person of merit his merit." In this world, the good provision (matā' ḥasan) is sometimes in terms of its kind and sometimes in terms of its quantity. And in the Hereafter it will be in terms of both kind and quantity, and it will be of such a degree that no one can even imagine it. However, we wish to say something about the good provision of this world.

In this world we see that many pious, righteous and repentant people, with great hardship and bitterness, keep body and soul together in this worldly life, although these verses contain a clear promise from Allah of good provision. We hear this question from countless people.

To understand the meaning contained in this verse, it is necessary that we try to understand life in its broader sense, seeking to understand it beyond its apparent circumstances and according to a wider and deeper meaning.

The reality is that in any society in which a righteous system is implemented, which is founded upon belief in Allah, in which obedience and submission are to Allah alone, in which Allah alone is recognised as the Lawgiver and Legislator, and in which people possess good deeds and character, then inevitably that society becomes developed, its facilities of life become abundant, and that society generally presents a model of a pure and clean life. In such a society every individual receives wages according to his effort. The members of that society are content, and prosperity is attained by them. And on the contrary, when we see that in some society the righteous and pure-natured people are passing their time with great difficulty, and they are counted among those deprived of goods and sources of sustenance, then the inevitable situation will be that the edifice of that society is not built upon belief in Allah, its system is not just, and in that entire society no person receives compensation according to his effort.

But it is also a reality that if righteous and virtuous people are living a narrow and bitter life in terms of wealth and sustenance, and oppression is being inflicted upon them by the society in which they exist, and they are being pursued from every side, as the polytheists of Makkah were inflicting oppression upon a small community of Muslims at the time of the revelation of this surah, and as every jahiliyyah always treats the bearers of the call of Islam in this same way, then we can say that these people are living a good life. This is not merely an idea or a claim, because connection with Allah, tranquillity of heart, peace from the Hereafter, and hope in the grace and mercy of Allah are in reality better provision. And for those people whose gaze rises a little above sensory and material life, this spiritual wealth is a greater good provision.

We do not say this because those people who do not receive, justly and equitably, their wages and good provision in accordance with their labour should abandon the struggle for good provision. For Islam never accepts oppression. And seeing such circumstances, a believer can never remain silent; Islam demands of a believing individual and a believing community that they continue the effort and struggle to change such conditions, so that righteous and virtuous workers may obtain good provision in accordance with their labour. Rather, we say that a righteous individual should be conscious of his rights, and should not accept the situation in which he continues to act and to labour but is not given its recompense and wage. It is their duty to create conditions in which pious and God-fearing people receive their full rights.

"Wa yu'ti kulla dhī faḍlin faḍlah" (and to every person of merit, his merit be given). Some exegetes have restricted this to the merit of the Hereafter. I consider that it relates to both this world and the Hereafter, just as we have explained "al-matā' al-ḥasan." Every person of excellence receives a reward as soon as he manifests his excellence. He attains psychological and conscious happiness. Whether this merit is practical or financial, if it is for the sake of Allah, then the reward is received at that time. The reward that will be given by Allah for it will be merit upon merit and will be the best of recompense.

"Wa in tawallaw fa innī akhāfu 'alaykum 'adhāba yawmin kabīr" (and if you turn away, then I fear for you the punishment of a great and terrible day). This is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. Some exegetes have said that it refers to the punishment of the Day of Badr. But this view is not correct, because the phrase "yawm kabīr," if used without qualification, means the Day of Resurrection, and the following sentence strengthens this view.

"Ilā Allāhi marji'ukum" (to Allah is your return). Although the return is to Allah both in this world and the Hereafter, and every moment and every instant a person returns to Allah, yet according to Quranic expressions the intended meaning is the state after the life of this world.

"Wa huwa 'alā kulli shay'in qadīr" (and He has power over all things). This clause also indicates that the great day mentioned refers to the Day of Resurrection, because on it people will be raised again, which the polytheists of Arabia considered far-fetched, and therefore it was said that Allah has power over all things.
